mentions.quote: these Manu assigned to women

entities.description: The primordial lawgiver who assigned specific qualities and duties to women.
entities.justification: Manu is named as the authority who assigned inherent qualities to women, establishing him as the founding legislator of the Dharmashastra tradition.

mentions.quote: their nature, which was created by Prajapati at the beginning
the Dharma, created by Prajapati in the beginning

entities.description: The creator deity who fashioned the nature of women and established the primal Dharma of marriage.
entities.justification: Prajapati is invoked twice as the cosmic originator who created both female nature and the foundational law of marriage, grounding these human institutions in divine creation.

mentions.quote: Akshamala, born of a low womb, being united with Vasishtha
mentions.role: husband whose union elevated a low-born woman

entities.description: A celebrated Vedic sage whose union with Akshamala, a low-born woman, is cited as proof that a wife attains the status of her husband.
entities.justification: Vasishtha's marriage to the low-born Akshamala is explicitly cited as a precedent case demonstrating the doctrine that a woman attains her husband's excellence.

mentions.quote: Akshamala, born of a low womb, being united with Vasishtha, attained venerability
mentions.role: exemplar of low-born woman elevated by marriage

entities.description: A woman of low birth who attained venerability through her union with the sage Vasishtha.
entities.justification: Akshamala is named as a canonical exemplar supporting the text's doctrine that a woman acquires her husband's spiritual and social status.

mentions.quote: Sharangi with Mandapala, attained venerability

entities.description: A sage whose union with Sharangi is cited alongside Vasishtha-Akshamala as a parallel example of elevation through marriage.
entities.justification: Mandapala is cited in the same verse as Vasishtha to illustrate that women of low birth attain excellence through marriage to distinguished husbands.

mentions.quote: Sharangi with Mandapala, attained venerability
mentions.role: exemplar of low-born woman elevated by marriage

entities.description: A woman of low birth who attained venerability through union with the sage Mandapala.
entities.justification: Sharangi is named as a second exemplar, parallel to Akshamala, proving the doctrine that a wife rises to her husband's status.

mentions.quote: The knowers of old know this earth to be the wife of Prithu
mentions.role: mythological king whose relation to Earth is invoked

entities.description: The legendary king who is said to have 'tamed' the earth, establishing the mythological identity of the earth as his wife.
entities.justification: Prithu is invoked in the context of seed-and-field metaphorics to ground the proprietary claim over productive land in ancient cosmological precedent.

mentions.quote: while Vena was ruling
mentions.role: wicked king during whose reign niyoga was introduced

mentions.quote: He, the foremost of royal sages, while enjoying the whole earth in ancient times, created a mixing of the varnas
mentions.role: antecedent of the pronoun in the niyoga degradation passage

entities.description: A legendary wicked king whose degenerate rule caused the varna mixing and is associated with the introduction of the condemned niyoga custom.
entities.justification: Vena is named as the historical marker for the period when the practice of appointing widows was first introduced, framing niyoga as a degraded innovation tied to a corrupt reign.

mentions.quote: A king should follow the brilliant conduct of Indra
As Indra sends down rain for the four months of the rainy season
mentions.role: simile-model for a king's bestowal of favors

entities.description: The king of the gods, whose seasonal gift of rain is the model for a king's generous distribution of favors to his kingdom.
entities.justification: Indra is invoked as the first in a series of eight divine models whose cosmic functions map onto idealized royal conduct, illustrating the vow of Indra.

mentions.quote: of the Sun
As the Sun for eight months draws up water with its rays
mentions.role: simile for a king drawing taxes

entities.description: The sun deity whose eight-month cycle of drawing up moisture is the model for a king's systematic tax collection.
entities.justification: Surya's seasonal absorption of water is mapped directly onto the duty of a king to draw taxes, illustrating one of eight divine royal vows.

mentions.quote: of the Wind
on how a seed must not be sown by a man in the wife of another
mentions.role: attributed singer of verses about seed and propriety

mentions.quote: As the Wind moves, having entered all beings, so should he enter everywhere with his spies

entities.description: The wind deity whose pervasive movement through all beings is the model for a king's all-seeing network of spies.
entities.justification: Vayu is cited both as the attributed singer of ancient verses on seed-propriety and as the divine model for the king's intelligence vow, entering everywhere unseen.

mentions.quote: of Yama
As Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come

entities.description: The god of death and dharmic restraint whose impartial treatment of beloved and hated alike models the king's impartial punishment.
entities.justification: Yama's impartial enforcement of the time of death is mapped onto the king's duty to restrain subjects without partiality.

mentions.quote: of Varuna
As one is seen bound by the fetters of Varuna

entities.description: The Vedic deity of cosmic order and binding oaths, whose fetters model the king's power to bind and restrain sinners.
entities.justification: Varuna's mythological fetters are explicitly invoked as the model for the king's restraining vow toward the sinful.

mentions.quote: of the Moon
As men rejoice on seeing the full moon, so is that king in whom his subjects rejoice
mentions.role: simile for a king who brings joy to subjects

entities.description: The moon deity whose appearance brings joy to all beings, modeling the king who makes his subjects rejoice.
entities.justification: The full moon's effect of delight on all who see it is directly mapped onto the desirable quality of a king whose subjects rejoice in him.

mentions.quote: of Agni
He should be ever endowed with majesty, fiery towards sinful acts

entities.description: The fire deity whose blazing power models the king's fierce majesty and destructive force against wicked vassals.
entities.justification: Agni is listed among the eight divine models for kingship and implicitly underlies the instruction that the king must be 'fiery towards sinful acts.'

mentions.quote: and a king should follow the brilliant conduct of ... Earth
As the Earth supports all beings equally, so is the supporting of all beings the vow of the Earth for a king
mentions.role: simile for universal impartial royal support

mentions.quote: For this earth is called the eternal womb of beings
The knowers of old know this earth to be the wife of Prithu

entities.description: The earth deity who supports all beings equally and is the final divine model for ideal royal conduct, also invoked mythologically as Prithu's wife.
entities.justification: Earth is simultaneously the concluding divine model for kingship (equal support of all beings) and a cosmological figure in both the seed-and-field metaphor and the Prithu myth.

mentions.quote: it is not possible to achieve the suppression of sin without Daṇḍa
him too he should punish with Daṇḍa
mentions.role: punishment applied to the lapsed Dharmic subject

entities.description: The principle and instrument of royal punishment, presented as the essential mechanism by which sin is suppressed and social order maintained.
entities.justification: Danda is named as a technical concept across multiple verses as the irreplaceable instrument of royal law enforcement.

surface_names: sovereign and the minister, the city, the kingdom, the treasury and the army, and the ally

mentions.quote: The sovereign and the minister, the city, the kingdom, the treasury and the army, and the ally as well—these seven are the limbs of a kingdom
mentions.role: enumeration of the classical saptanga theory of the state

mentions.quote: But of these seven constituent elements of the kingdom, in their order, one should know the affliction of each preceding one is greater than the succeeding
mentions.role: hierarchy of state constituents by importance

mentions.quote: In this seven-limbed kingdom, which is supported like a three-staved staff

entities.description: The classical Indian political theory (saptanga) enumerating the seven constituent limbs of a kingdom and their ranked importance.
entities.justification: The saptanga doctrine is explicitly stated and elaborated over three consecutive verses, making it a central political-theoretical idea in this window.

mentions.quote: The Krita, the Treta, and the Dvapara, and the Kali as well—all these are the conduct of the king
mentions.role: cosmic ages mapped onto a king's wakefulness and action

mentions.quote: The Kali is when he is asleep; when he is awake, it is the Dvapara age; when he is ready for action, the Treta; but when he moves, he is the Krita
mentions.role: specific mapping of king's states to ages

entities.description: The four cosmic ages (Krita/Satya, Treta, Dvapara, Kali), here reinterpreted as corresponding to the four states of a king's wakefulness and activity.
entities.justification: The yuga system is explicitly invoked and reinterpreted as a metaphor for royal activity, condensing cosmic time into a theory of royal energy.

mentions.quote: desired offspring may be obtained by a woman, through niyoga (the appointment of a man to her)
those who are without a field but have seed
In the sacred formulas for marriage, niyoga is nowhere mentioned
This bestial law is condemned by the learned twice-born
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born

entities.description: The practice of appointing a man to beget offspring on a widow or childless wife, presented in this window as a degraded, condemned custom lacking Vedic authority.
entities.justification: Niyoga is the central contested institution in this chapter section, defined, provisionally described, then emphatically condemned as a bestial practice introduced during Vena's corrupt reign.

mentions.quote: Seeing this to be the highest Dharma for all varnas
mentions.role: universal applicability of wife-protection across all social orders

mentions.quote: created a mixing of the varnas
mentions.role: varna mixing as consequence of royal wickedness

entities.description: The four-fold social order whose maintenance is a core concern of this chapter, with varna-mixing treated as a sign of civilizational decay.
entities.justification: Varna is invoked both as the universal frame for the duty of wife-protection and as the social order whose disruption marks the depth of Vena's transgression.

mentions.quote: she obtains the womb of a jackal and is afflicted by terrible diseases
mentions.role: degraded rebirth destination for an unfaithful wife

entities.description: The jackal as a degraded animal womb into which an unfaithful wife is reborn as karmic punishment.
entities.justification: The jackal is named as the specific animal rebirth that awaits an adulterous wife, functioning as a concrete marker of moral degradation in the karmic economy.

mentions.quote: If a bull should beget a hundred calves in the cows of others

entities.description: A bull used as a concrete legal analogy to establish that offspring belong to the owner of the mother, not the sire.
entities.justification: The bull-and-cow analogy is the primary illustration for the property-law principle that calves (children) belong to the owner of the cows (wife/field), not the sire.

themes.topic: Female subordination and control as religious and social duty

mentions.quote: Women must be made dependent by their men day and night
a woman is never fit for independence
There is no rite for women with sacred formulas; this is the established rule in Dharma

themes.justification: The opening third of this window is structured around the thesis that women must be kept dependent by fathers, husbands, and sons, and this subordination is framed as the supreme Dharma.

themes.topic: Seed and field metaphysics of procreation and property

mentions.quote: The woman is remembered as the field, the man is remembered as the seed
of the seed and of the womb, the seed is said to be more excellent
If a bull should beget a hundred calves in the cows of others, those calves belong to the owners of the cows

themes.justification: An extended metaphysical-legal argument runs from paragraph 32 to 54 deploying the seed-field-crop analogy to resolve questions of paternity, property, and reproductive rights.

themes.topic: Condemnation of niyoga as a bestial, non-Vedic deviation

mentions.quote: This bestial law is condemned by the learned twice-born
In the sacred formulas for marriage, niyoga is nowhere mentioned
From that time onwards, he who, out of delusion, appoints a woman whose husband is dead for the sake of offspring, him they call a fool

themes.justification: After tentatively describing niyoga rules, the text pivots to an emphatic condemnation, framing the practice as historically contingent, lacking Vedic authority, and associated with Vena's corrupt reign.

themes.topic: Chastity and fidelity as the path to the husband's world after death

mentions.quote: She who does not transgress against her husband, being controlled in mind, speech, and body, she attains her husband's world
through infidelity to her husband, a woman obtains condemnation in the world; she obtains the womb of a jackal
With a husband of whatever quality a woman is united according to the rule, of that same quality she becomes, like a river entering the ocean

themes.justification: The karma of marital fidelity—heavenly reward and elevation of status versus jackal-rebirth and disease—is a sustained eschatological concern in the first half of this window.

themes.topic: Kingly duty of protection, intelligence, and just punishment

mentions.quote: A king, whose eye is his spies, should know two kinds of thieves who take the property of others
it is not possible to achieve the suppression of sin without Daṇḍa
A king should have such places patrolled by stationary and moving detachments of troops, and also by spies

themes.justification: The second half of this window pivots entirely to kingship, detailing how the king should use spies, surveillance, just punishment, and graduated penalties to suppress crime and maintain order.

themes.topic: The king as microcosm of the eight divine cosmic principles

mentions.quote: A king should follow the brilliant conduct of Indra, of the Sun, of the Wind, of Yama, of Varuna, of the Moon, of Agni, and of Earth
The Krita, the Treta, and the Dvapara, and the Kali as well—all these are the conduct of the king

themes.justification: The window closes with a theological-political theory mapping eight deities' cosmic functions onto royal duties, presenting the king as the earthly embodiment of divine cosmic order.

themes.topic: Graduated and proportional punishment as the basis of dharmic governance

mentions.quote: Having proclaimed their faults in their respective occupations in truth, the king should inflict punishment justly, according to the Shastra
For a cut-purse, he should have his fingers cut off at the first offense; at the second, his hand and foot; at the third, he should be slain
For all physicians who practice falsely, the punishment is the first amercement for non-human creatures, but the middle amercement for human beings

themes.justification: A detailed penal code runs through paragraphs 80–112, specifying escalating or proportional punishments for a wide range of offenses, constituting a systematic theory of graduated dharmic justice.

themes.topic: The inheritance of qualities through procreation and marital union

mentions.quote: whatever kind of man a woman consorts with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, of that same kind it grows there
women of low birth in this world have attained excellence by the auspicious qualities of their respective husbands

themes.justification: The text develops a quasi-biological theory of quality-transmission through both maternal contact and seed, applying it to social hierarchy, rebirth, and the elevation of low-born women.

themes.topic: Taxation as the king's dharmic appropriation of the kingdom's produce

mentions.quote: As the Sun for eight months draws up water with its rays, so should he constantly draw taxes from his kingdom; for that is the vow of the Sun
As Indra sends down rain for the four months of the rainy season, so should he shower his kingdom with favors

themes.justification: The solar-lunar cycle of extraction and return implicitly structures a complete theory of taxation: the king draws resources like the sun (eight months) and redistributes like Indra's rain (four months).

citations.quote: There is no rite for women with sacred formulas; this is the established rule in Dharma. For women are without strength and without Vedic formulas
citations.justification: The Vedas are implicitly cited as the source of the absence of women's rites, with the Vedic formula being the authoritative standard that women fall short of.

citations.quote: many Vedic texts are also sung in the Vedas for the examination of their own nature
citations.justification: The Vedas are explicitly invoked as the textual authority for understanding women's nature, framing the following quotation as a Vedic citation.

citations.quote: Whatever sin my mother committed, wandering about as an unchaste wife, may my father take that seed of mine—this is the Vedic formula for reclamation of the seed
citations.justification: A specific Vedic formula is quoted verbatim as a textual authority legitimizing the father's claim over offspring even in cases of the mother's infidelity.

citations.cited_work: Verses sung by the Wind (attributed oral tradition)
citations.quote: those who know the past recite verses sung by the Wind, on how a seed must not be sown by a man in the wife of another
citations.justification: A body of verses attributed to Vayu is cited as an ancient oral authority supporting the prohibition on sowing seed in another man's wife.
